title: The influence of antenatal and pregnancy-related factors on recovery after childbirth: a systematic review
authors: Zayël Z. Frijmersum; Eva Van der Meij; Ralph De Vries; Johannes R. Anema; Judith A.F. Huirne; Petra C.A.M. Bakker
pain_condition_detail: Persistent postpartum genitopelvic or postsurgical pain, urinary incontinence, functional ability, and postpartum mental health outcomes.
context_note: The review frames maternal morbidity as a public health issue and includes English- or Dutch-language studies, but does not report a single country or healthcare system.
bps_function_set: background framing; conclusion; intervention rationale; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: It operationalizes BPS mainly through ICF: recovery outcomes are grouped into physical, mental, functional, and social participation domains, and factors into seven antenatal/pregnancy categories. The paper reports associations and recommends tailored care, but it does not define BPS variables, test a model, or specify cross-domain mechanisms.
integration_mechanism_summary: None proposed. The paper reports associations and recommends combining exercise, mental health support, and workplace adaptations, but does not specify a biological, psychological, or social pathway linking them.
bps_model_variants_3: biopsychosocial approach to antenatal and postpartum care
conceptual_tensions_1: The review’s BPS/ICF framing includes social participation, but no included studies assessed it
conceptual_tensions_2: Physical recovery is the most frequently assessed domain, while functional ability and social participation are underrepresented
conceptual_tensions_3: Physical activity is protective in some included studies but null or adverse in others
conceptual_tensions_4: Age thresholds and outcome definitions vary, limiting comparability across studies
conceptual_tensions_5: Biomedical outcomes dominate despite the stated aim to assess recovery as multidimensional
additional_observations_1: The ICF framework organizes outcomes into physical, mental, functional, and social participation domains, BPS is not converted into measured variables
additional_observations_2: Narrative synthesis was used because study heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis
additional_observations_3: The paper treats lifestyle as a separate category rather than as a pathway linking biological, psychological, and social domains
additional_observations_4: Quality assessment used NOS and RoB 2, no AMSTAR, ROBIS, or GRADE tool is named
additional_observations_5: Social support is framed as potentially modifiable, but only one eligible study evaluated it
additional_observations_6: The paper recommends combining prenatal exercise, mental health support, and workplace adaptations without specifying how these components interact
synthesis_note: The review uses ICF to operationalize a multidimensional recovery frame and groups factors into biomedical, psychological, social, and lifestyle categories. It reports many associations, especially psychological predictors of pain/functional outcomes, but does not define a BPS mechanism or test variables; social participation is absent from included evidence.
coding_rationale: Domains are mostly parallel, with strongest psych-bio and psych-social associations. Social participation is underrepresented. No triadic mechanism is specified.

title: The influence of antenatal and pregnancy-related factors on recovery after childbirth: a systematic review
authors: Zayël Z. Frijmersum; Eva Van der Meij; Ralph De Vries; Johannes R. Anema; Judith A.F. Huirne; Petra C.A.M. Bakker
context_note: Published in AJOG Global Reports 2026; English and Dutch studies included; PROSPERO registered.
bps_function_set: background framing; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The review uses the biopsychosocial label as an organizing principle to structure the identification of antenatal and pregnancy-related factors affecting postpartum recovery, but does not define the model or demonstrate integration between biological, psychological, and social domains.
conceptual_tensions_1: The review uses the biopsychosocial label extensively but does not demonstrate integration between biological, psychological, and social domains
conceptual_tensions_2: Conflicting findings on lifestyle factors (e.g., prenatal exercise) suggest context-dependent effects that are not fully explained
conceptual_tensions_3: The ICF framework conceptualizes recovery as multidimensional, but the evidence base lacks studies on social participation outcomes
additional_observations_1: The review focuses exclusively on antenatal and pregnancy-related factors, excluding delivery-related factors which were addressed in a separate review by the same group
additional_observations_2: Pain catastrophizing was measured using a scale, but the specific instrument was not named in the text
additional_observations_3: The review acknowledges that outcomes related to anatomic changes were only included if linked to morbidity, potentially limiting representation of certain biological factors
synthesis_note: This systematic review identifies antenatal and pregnancy-related factors affecting postpartum recovery using the ICF framework. While the biopsychosocial label is used throughout, there is no demonstrated integration between domains. Psychological factors are most elaborated, with biological and social factors mentioned but not integrated. Key gaps include lack of studies on social participation and heterogeneous measurement of functional ability. The review recommends a biopsychosocial approach to care despite not operationalizing the model's integrative potential.
coding_rationale: The review uses BPS as an organizing principle without demonstrating domain integration. Psychological domain is elaborated through multiple constructs; biological and social are mentioned but not linked. BPS typology is 'multifactorial' - all three domains present but treated in parallel.
biological_factors_01_factor_verbatim: Five studies found that women who experienced lumbopelvic pain in pregnancy were significantly more likely to experience persistent pelvic pain after childbirth (P <.05).
biological_factors_02_factor_verbatim: Three studies reported that a high BMI was associated with increased risk of persistent lumbopelvic pain after childbirth (OR, 1.5; 95% CI, 1.2–2.0; P =.018) and urinary incontinence (OR, 1.94; 95% CI, 1.20–3.14; P =.007).
biological_factors_03_factor_verbatim: Two studies reported significantly higher risk of persistent pelvic and post–cesarean delivery site pain among women who smoked during pregnancy (OR, 1.2; 95% CI, 1.0–1.4; adjusted relative risk, 2.22; 95% CI, 1.27–3.88; P <.05).
biological_factors_04_factor_verbatim: One study reported that excessive nausea and vomiting during pregnancy was associated with persistent pelvic pain (OR, 2.83; 95% CI, 2.25–3.57), whereas another found a higher risk of postpartum emotional distress (P =.001).
